evidence.label: Exponential PSD rank of positively shifted matching matrices

headline: Exact semidefinite descriptions of perfect matching need exponential size, a new paper claims.
scope: The bound covers exact descriptions only, with a fixed shift strictly between 0 and 1 and large even n.
plain: The perfect matching polytope is a shape whose corners are the ways to pair up n people. One can try to describe it as the shadow of a bigger object built from positive semidefinite matrices. This paper claims to prove that any such exact description needs matrices whose size grows exponentially in n. Earlier proofs covered only linear descriptions, or semidefinite ones with built-in symmetry. Lean has checked weaker versions that give growth faster than any polynomial.
doesNot: This does not rule out small semidefinite descriptions that are only approximately correct.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: If it holds, it extends Rothvoss's linear bound for matching to every exact semidefinite description.

explanation:
Six people must split into three pairs. There are 15 ways to do it. Each way is called a perfect matching. Now circle three of the six, say persons 1, 2 and 3. A group with an odd number of people is an odd set. Some pairs then cross the circle, with one partner inside and one outside. Of the 15 matchings, 9 have exactly one crossing pair and 6 have three. None has zero or two. An odd set always forces an odd number of crossings.

Now build a table with one row per odd set and one column per matching. Six people have 32 odd sets: 6 singles, 20 triples and 6 groups of five. So the table has 32 rows, 15 columns and 480 cells. Pick a fixed shift ρ (the Greek letter rho) between 0 and 1. In each cell, write the number of crossing pairs, minus 1, plus ρ. With ρ = 1/2, 360 cells hold 0.5 and 120 cells hold 2.5. The paper studies this table for every even number n of people.

The table comes from geometry. Write each matching as a list of 0s and 1s, one entry per possible pair. These lists are the corners of a shape called the perfect matching polytope. In 1965 Jack Edmonds described this shape with simple inequalities. Many of them say that each odd set has at least one crossing pair. The table with ρ = 0 records each corner's slack (how far it sits from each such wall).

How compactly can the shape be described? One way is a lift: show the shape as the shadow of a simpler object in more dimensions. A semidefinite lift builds that object from positive semidefinite matrices. These are symmetric square grids of numbers whose matching quadratic expression is never negative. The lift's size is the side length of the grids. Gouveia, Parrilo and Thomas linked the smallest size to one number of the slack table. It is the table's positive semidefinite rank, or PSD rank. That is the smallest r for which each row and each column gets an r-by-r such matrix. Pairing a row's matrix with a column's matrix must give the cell's value exactly.

At ρ = 1 a cheap recipe exists. Use one diagonal slot per possible pair, which gives 15 slots for six people. A row's matrix marks the pairs that cross its odd set. A column's matrix marks the pairs in its matching. Pairing them counts crossing pairs, which is the cell's value when ρ = 1. This size grows only like n squared. The paper notes that ρ = 1 must therefore be left out of its result.

The earlier work all used simpler kinds of recipe. In 1991 Mihalis Yannakakis built the factorization framework. He proved an exponential bound for symmetric linear descriptions. In 2017 Thomas Rothvoss proved the exponential bound for all linear descriptions. Semidefinite lifts can be far smaller than linear ones, so that bound does not carry over. Braun and Pokutta handled this shifted table in 2015, with plain nonnegative numbers in place of matrices. Braun and coauthors proved exponential bounds for symmetric semidefinite descriptions in 2017. Lee, Raghavendra and Steurer gave a general method for unrestricted semidefinite bounds in 2015. This paper follows their method.

The single obstacle is that the matrices may be anything. No symmetry, sparsity or limited precision is assumed. The proof must average a row's matrix over many cuts, but averages and squares do not trade places. The paper instead writes each average exactly as a sum of squares and controls those pieces. The contradiction comes from an impossible parity puzzle, built into groups of people inside the matching.

The paper claims to prove that the shifted table has exponential PSD rank. There is one constant c above zero that works for every fixed ρ strictly between 0 and 1. For large even n, the rank is at least 2 to the power cn. As a consequence, the unshifted table also has exponential rank. So every exact semidefinite lift of the perfect matching polytope would have exponential size. Compare that with the 15 slots, or n squared growth, available at ρ = 1.

Three limits matter. The paper gives no number for c. It takes c = 1/(2k), where k is a large fixed group size that is never computed. The size of n where the bound starts depends on ρ. And exactness is essential. Kaniewski, Lee and de Wolf built tables of smaller than exponential PSD rank that match the unshifted table almost exactly. Their entries miss by at most 2 to the power minus the square root of n/2.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked weaker versions, according to the Lean scope note. Pick any fixed power C. For large even n, a perfect-matching slack table has PSD rank above n to the power C. Every exact semidefinite lift likewise needs size above n to the power C. That is faster than any polynomial, but it is not the exponential bound for every shift. The exponential claim lies outside that check. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. Lean checks only weaker, faster-than-polynomial versions, not the exponential bound. The constant c is never computed, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A way to split all the points of a group into pairs.
A group with an odd number of the points; some pair must cross its boundary.
The shape whose corners are all perfect matchings, each written as a list of 0s and 1s.
How far a corner of a shape sits from one of the walls that bound it.
A symmetric square grid of numbers whose matching quadratic expression is never negative.
A description of a shape as the shadow of a slice of positive semidefinite matrices; its size is their side length.
The smallest matrix size that lets every table cell be written exactly as a pairing of a row matrix and a column matrix.
